title: Esca
excerpt: Esca is short for escaleren. Dutch students use it for a night or party that was a lot of fun.
example: "What an esca last night," he texted the group the next morning.
text: You use it looking back on a night that got out of hand. In a good way. Think dancing on tables, not calling the ambu. The English word lit comes close.

title: Escaleren
excerpt: Escaleren (to escalate) means a night turned into a big, fun success. In Dutch student slang it is a good thing.
example: What started as a quiet dinner escalated until deep into the night.
text: In normal life escalating sounds bad. Among Dutch students it is the goal of every night out. Some call it kantelen. The only condition: you don't end up taking the rattentaxi home early.

title: Esma
excerpt: Esma is Dutch student slang for an espresso martini.
example: At the borrel she ordered an esma instead of a beer for a change.
text: The cocktail is vodka, coffee liqueur and a shot of espresso, served in a martini glass with a few coffee beans on top. Party and caffeine in one. Dutch students love shortening drink names, see also baco and cappu.

title: Eventuela
excerpt: An eventuela is someone you might want a relationship with, but you are not sure yet.
example: "Is that just a scharrel or secretly your eventuela?" her housemate asked.
text: It comes from "eventueel", which means possibly. If things grow, an eventuela can become a prela and in the end a real rela. Dutch students have a word for every stage of dating.

title: Exchange student
excerpt: An exchange student studies in another country for a while, as part of an exchange programme.
example: "Twenty exchange students are coming to view our house this semester. Better teach them the word gezellig."
text: An exchange student stays enrolled at their own university, but takes courses abroad for a while. Often through Erasmus. For lots of students it is one of the best times of their student years. Dutch students jokingly call internationals internacho.

title: Exclu
excerpt: Exclu is Dutch slang for being exclusive: the stage where you only date each other.
example: "So are you two exclu now or still just a scharrel?" she asked straight out.
text: Exclu is short for "exclusief". Dutch students use the short version just as often as the full word. It usually comes right after the DTR talk.

title: Exclusive
excerpt: Being exclusive means you only see and sleep with each other, without calling it a relationship yet.
example: After a few weeks they agreed to be exclusive, without putting a label on it right away.
text: It is an in-between stage. You only date each other, but it is not an official relationship with everything that comes with it. Dutch students call it exclusief, or just exclu.

title: Extern
excerpt: Extern is someone or something from outside your own student association or student house.
example: For the party everyone was allowed to bring an extern.
text: The word separates members or housemates from outsiders at an activity or borrel. As an international you might be the extern at first. Don't worry, it doesn't take long to become one of the group.

title: FaceTune
excerpt: FaceTune is a photo editing app. The name is also used for selfies that are heavily edited.
example: "He looks totally different on Instagram than in real life. I think everything is facetuned."
text: With the app you can smooth your skin, slim your face or change your body. When someone says a photo is facetuned, they mean it was edited a lot. It is like a heavy filter.

title: Facts
excerpt: You say facts when you completely agree with what someone says. Exactly, that's how it is.
example: "Monday morning lectures at half past eight should be illegal." "Facts."
text: Facts is a short reaction, like "exactly" or "so true". You use it to say something is simply right. It is close to real or period.

title: Feut
excerpt: A feut is a prospective member of a Dutch student association who still has to get through the introduction period.
example: As a feut she had to accept every drink from the older members that night.
text: The name comes from foetus, as in not fully grown yet. Before a feut becomes a full member, they have to get through the KMT, the introduction period. Some associations call them AL. Once you are in, you laugh about it.

title: Filter
excerpt: A filter is a digital effect that changes how a photo or video looks.
example: "I'm not posting a selfie without a filter. After that party I look like a zombie."
text: A filter can just change colours or lighting. But there are also filters that change your face or add dog ears and a nose. Some are so strong you can barely recognise the person.

title: FinSta
excerpt: A FinSta is a fake Instagram. A second, private account you only share with close friends.
example: "That photo of me asleep on the train? That's only on my FinSta."
text: Despite the word fake, a FinSta is where you post the real, unfiltered stuff. Your main account is your "rinsta", your real Instagram. A FinSta is basically a kind of alt account.

title: Fire
excerpt: Fire means something is really good, cool or impressive.
example: "That new DJ at the soos? Fire. I danced all night."
text: Fire is a broad compliment. It can be about music, food, outfits or parties. Usually with a flame emoji. It is close to lit and bussin.

title: Fit check
excerpt: A fit check is a quick look at, or review of, someone's outfit.
example: "Fit check for the gala! Is this okay or should I wear the other shoes?"
text: Fit is short for outfit. Fit checks are often mirror videos or short clips showing clothes, shoes and accessories. On TikTok people show what they are wearing that way. It is close to OOTD.

title: Flaneren
excerpt: Flaneren means walking around to be seen, for example at the sociëteit or in town.
example: In his new suit he strolled confidently through the sociëteit.
text: The goal is simple: look and be seen. Dutch students do it at the sociëteit, in town or on the street during a night out. It comes from the French flâner. Basically a slow victory lap with no victory.

title: Flatmate
excerpt: A flatmate is someone you share a flat or student house with. A housemate.
example: "My flatmate ate all my eggs again without asking."
text: Flatmate is mostly British English. It is like roommate, but you don't share a bedroom. You live in the same place and share the kitchen and bathroom. In Dutch student houses you often have a whole bunch of flatmates.

title: Flex
excerpt: Flexing means showing off what you have or what you can do.
example: "He showed off his new watch a lot tonight. Big flex."
text: Flexing comes from tensing your muscles to show them off. Now it is about money, clothes, trips or achievements. A weird flex is bragging about something that isn't impressive at all.

title: Flip cup
excerpt: Flip cup is a team drinking game. You empty your cup and then try to flip it over with one tap.
example: "Flip cup, boys against girls. The losing team does the dishes."
text: In flip cup two teams face each other at a table. You drink your cup, put it on the edge and tap it until it lands upside down. Only then can your teammate go. It is a fast relay race.

title: FML
excerpt: FML stands for fuck my life. You use it when something goes wrong, is embarrassing or when you have bad luck.
example: "Bike stolen, phone dead and it's raining. FML."
text: FML is rude and casual, but usually meant dramatically. You use it for small disasters, like missing the train or sleeping through an exam. Getting your bike stolen in the Netherlands is basically a canon event.

title: FOMO
excerpt: FOMO stands for fear of missing out. It is the fear of missing something fun, so you go to every party anyway.
example: Even though she had an exam the next day, she went to the party out of pure FOMO.
text: FOMO makes you go to a party or borrel instead of staying home, even when you are tired or should be studying. The opposite is JOMO, the joy of missing out.

title: Frat
excerpt: Frat is short for fraternity. An American student association, traditionally for men.
example: "He joined a frat during his exchange. Now he only wears caps."
text: A fraternity is about friendship, parties, networking and sometimes charity. Members often live together in a frat house. The closest Dutch thing is a studentenvereniging or a dispuut. The female version is a sorority.

title: Frat party
excerpt: A frat party is a party thrown by an American student fraternity.
example: "Red cups, beer pong and way too loud music. It felt like a real frat party."
text: Frat parties are famous from American films. They usually happen in the fraternity house. Big crowds, lots of drinks and drinking games. In the Netherlands a party at the soos comes closest.

title: Fresher
excerpt: A fresher is a first-year university student, especially in the UK.
example: "You can tell she's a fresher. She's asking for the library with a map in her hand."
text: Fresher is the British word for a first-year. The American version is freshman. In the Netherlands first-years are called sjaars. Freshers start their studies with Freshers' Week.

title: Freshers' Week
excerpt: Freshers' Week is the welcome week for new students, especially in the UK.
example: "After Freshers' Week I knew a hundred new people. I don't remember a single name."
text: During Freshers' Week universities and student unions organise parties, meetups and fairs for clubs and societies. Lots of new students call it the best week of the year. The Dutch version is the introductieweek.

title: Freshman
excerpt: A freshman is a first-year student at an American high school or university.
example: "In his freshman year in California he lived in a dorm with three others."
text: Freshman is typically American. After that you become a sophomore, a junior and a senior. Some schools prefer the neutral first-year student. In the UK they say fresher.

title: Friendzone
excerpt: Being in the friendzone means you want more, but the other person only sees you as a friend.
example: "She said I'm like a brother to her. Officially friendzoned."
text: The friendzone is a frustrating place for a lot of people. You are close, but it never turns romantic. Whoever stays there for ages and does everything for the other person quickly gets called a simp.

title: Fuif
excerpt: A fuif is a party with a relaxed, homey vibe. The word is mostly used in Belgium and the south of the Netherlands.
example: They threw a fun fuif in the garden of the student house, with their own DJ.
text: A fuif is a bit more casual than a big event. Think a party in a student house, a garden or a local hall. In Flanders it is the standard word for a student party. Further north you will hear it less.

title: Fusie
excerpt: Fusie is Dutch student slang for the shared living room of a student house.
example: Every evening at seven everyone sat down in the fusie for dinner together.
text: It is the place where housemates run into each other most. Eating together, watching TV or just catching up. Depending on the city it is also called the GR, GK or geru. Same room, different name.

title: FWB
excerpt: FWB stands for friends with benefits: friends who sleep together without being in a relationship.
example: They agreed clearly that they would just stay FWB, without any expectations.
text: Friendship and sex combined, without the commitments of a real relationship. Often, but not always, FWBs stay exclusive with each other. It works great. Until someone catches feelings.

title: FYI
excerpt: FYI stands for for your information.
example: "FYI, tomorrow's lecture is cancelled. Check the group chat."
text: With FYI you share something the other person should know. Depending on the tone it sounds helpful or a bit passive aggressive. Like: "FYI, it was your turn to do the dishes."

title: FYP
excerpt: FYP stands for For You Page. It is the personal feed on TikTok that the algorithm puts together for you.
example: "How did my FYP suddenly turn into only cats and recipes?"
text: Your FYP shows videos the algorithm thinks you will like. Creators often add #fyp to their videos, hoping they end up on more pages. What you watch and like decides what you see next.

title: Galaplicht
excerpt: Galaplicht (gala duty) is the unwritten, and very debated, idea that a gala date means more than just dancing.
example: "Forget the galaplicht," she said, "I'm just going for a fun night."
text: Dutch student associations throw formal galas, and everyone brings a date. Galaplicht is the old joke that this comes with obligations afterwards. In reality nobody owes anybody anything. A fun night is the whole point.

title: Gap year
excerpt: A gap year is a year between school, studies or work in which you do something else.
example: "After my exams I'm taking a gap year. First six months of backpacking through South America."
text: People use a gap year to travel, work, volunteer or figure out what they want. In the Netherlands it is called a tussenjaar. Afterwards you often start your studies with more motivation.

title: Gaslighting
excerpt: Gaslighting is manipulating someone so much that they start doubting their own memory or feelings.
example: "I never said that. You're making things up again. You're way too sensitive."
text: The term comes from the 1944 film Gaslight, where a man makes his wife believe she is going mad. Gaslighting is a serious form of manipulation in relationships. Online the word is sometimes used too easily for normal arguments.

title: Gefeli
excerpt: Gefeli is Dutch student slang for "gefeliciteerd": congratulations.
example: "Gefeli with your propedeuse!" was written in big letters on the homemade cake.
text: You mostly see it in texts and on birthday cards, where the full word feels a bit too formal. Dutch people congratulate everyone at a birthday, including the family of the birthday person. So you will need this one a lot.

title: Geru
excerpt: Geru is short for "gemeenschappelijke ruimte", the shared living room of a Dutch student house.
example: After class everyone sat down in the geru again for an episode on the couch.
text: Depending on the city you also hear GR, GK or fusie for the same room. The meaning is always the same. It is where the house hangs out, eats and argues about the dishes.

title: Gezel
excerpt: Gezel is short for gezellig, the famous Dutch word for cosy, fun and nice to be around.
example: "So gezel that you're joining us tonight," she said with a big smile.
text: Gezellig has no perfect English translation. It is the warm feeling of a good time with good people. Students shorten it to gezel. Or gezellie, when they want to sound extra enthusiastic.

title: Ghost account
excerpt: A ghost account is an account with almost no posts, info or activity. It is only used to look around.
example: "Someone without a profile picture watches all my stories. Probably a ghost account of my ex."
text: People use ghost accounts to quietly look around or protect their privacy. You see the profile, but nothing happens on it. It goes hand in hand with lurking: always watching, never reacting.

title: Ghosting
excerpt: Ghosting means suddenly cutting off all contact without any explanation. You disappear like a ghost.
example: "We had three great dates and since then I haven't heard anything. I got ghosted."
text: When someone ghosts you, they stop texting, calling and replying. No fight, no goodbye. It happens a lot in dating, but in friendships too. For the person who gets ghosted it usually feels bad and confusing.

title: GinTo
excerpt: GinTo is Dutch student slang for a gin and tonic.
example: On the sunny terrace she ordered a GinTo without a second thought.
text: The short version isn't that much shorter. But it just sounds a lot more studentikoos. The go-to terrace drink once the first sunny day of spring arrives.

title: GK
excerpt: GK stands for "gemeenschappelijke kamer", the shared room of a Dutch student house. The same as a GR or fusie.
example: In their house they always called the living room the GK instead of the geru.
text: It is always the same room. Which name you use mostly depends on the city you live in. Ask your new housemates which one they use. Using the wrong one marks you as new.

title: Glazing
excerpt: Glazing means praising someone way too much. Over the top compliments.
example: "Stop glazing. He just passed an exam, he didn't win a Nobel Prize."
text: Glazing comes from the glaze on a doughnut. You are covering someone in praise. The word got popular on TikTok around 2022 and is often used for fans who never look at their idol critically.

title: Glow-up
excerpt: A glow-up is a big change for the better in someone's looks, confidence or life.
example: "Did you see his photo from the reunion? What a glow-up since secondary school."
text: You often see a glow-up in before and after photos. It can be about looks, but also about becoming happier, healthier or more confident. A glow-up after a breakup is a classic.

title: GOAT
excerpt: GOAT stands for Greatest Of All Time. The best ever at something.
example: "She got a nine for statistics without going to a single lecture. Truly the GOAT."
text: The abbreviation comes from sports. Messi and Ronaldo often get called the GOAT. You also use it for friends who do something great for you. Usually with a goat emoji.

title: Goos
excerpt: Goos is another word for gozer: a mate, or sometimes an idiot.
example: "Hey goos, are you joining us?" he shouted across the room.
text: Depending on the tone it can be friendly or mocking. Context is everything. Said with a grin, it is a mate. Said with an eye roll, not so much.

title: Gozer
excerpt: Gozer is Dutch slang for a guy or mate. Or an idiot, depending on the context.
example: "Calm down, gozer," she said when he made another dumb joke.
text: The same word can be affectionate or a light insult. It all depends on how you say it. A bit like "mate" in British English, which can also go both ways.

title: GPA
excerpt: GPA stands for Grade Point Average. The average grade of your study results, mostly used in the US.
example: "For that master in the US I have to convert my grades into a GPA."
text: Your GPA is a number on a scale, usually from 0 to 4. The higher, the better. American universities and employers look at it a lot. In the Netherlands grades go from 1 to 10, and a 6 already means you passed.

title: GR
excerpt: GR stands for "gemeenschappelijke ruimte", the shared living room of a Dutch student house.
example: On Friday nights the GR was always packed with housemates and their friends.
text: Depending on the city you also hear GK or fusie for the same room. The GR is the heart of the house. Every borrel, dinner and late-night talk happens there.

title: Green flag
excerpt: A green flag is a good sign. Behaviour that shows someone is good for you.
example: "He asked if I got home safely. Green flag."
text: Green flags are things like being honest, listening well and respecting your boundaries. People share lists of their favourite green flags online. The opposite is a red flag.
